A.title: Type and Stringency of Campylobacter Microbiological Criterion (PHC vs. FSC)

A1.title: Status quo PHC
A1.description: Maintain the existing PHC only (no FSC). Continue relying on process controls and corrective actions without imposing batch-based market prohibitions.

A2.title: Phased FSC (lenient limit)
A2.description: Introduce an FSC with a relatively high limit and c>0 acceptance, phased in gradually with risk-based sampling. This would ease adaptation for SMEs and reduce waste.

A3.title: Risk-based FSC (moderate limit)
A3.description: Establish an FSC aligned to public health targets, with mandatory batch actions when limits are exceeded. Apply risk-based sampling frequency and implement targeted waste mitigation measures.

A4.title: Strict FSC (low limit & immediate enforcement)
A4.description: Adopt a stringent FSC with a low limit and immediate withdrawal or recall of non-compliant batches to maximize public health protection.

B.title: Primary control focus along the supply chain

B1.title: Processing & Retail Focus
B1.description: Concentrate efforts on enhancing hygiene practices and implementing advanced decontamination technologies at processing facilities, while also improving retail standards and transparency to ensure product safety. This approach aims to reduce contamination in the supply chain and provide consumers with clear information on poultry safety, without focusing primarily on on-farm interventions.

B2.title: Process-first
B2.description: Prioritize slaughterhouse and processing controls, including decontamination technologies, as the main points for risk reduction.

B3.title: Balanced multi-hurdle
B3.description: Distribute control measures and investment evenly across the farm, processing, retail, and consumer stages.

B4.title: Consumer & transparency focus
B4.description: Center efforts on labeling, behavior change, and transparency initiatives to reduce household-level contamination risks.

B5.title: Environment-first
B5.description: Emphasize control of environmental leakage (e.g., runoff, vectors, VBNC survival) and enforce tighter environmental safeguards.

C.title: Cost burden sharing and food-waste mitigation mechanisms

C1.title: Producer liability
C1.description: Industry bears full compliance and non-compliance costs. Failed batches follow standard disposal routes without subsidies. Additional costs cannot be passed to the consumer

C2.title: Targeted public co-funding
C2.description: Provide temporary public financial support (subsidies or tax credits) for validated control measures and SME adaptation, to prevent consumer price increases.

C3.title: Regulated pass-through with transparency
C3.description: Permit cost pass-through to consumers, conditional on transparent reporting and performance benchmarking by retailers. There will be no subsidies or tax credits

C4.title: Waste-minimization toolkit
C4.description: Fund innovations such as dynamic shelf-life management, reprocessing or valorization options, and case-by-case batch risk assessment to reduce avoidable waste.

C5.title: Balanced cost-sharing compact
C5.description: Combine producer obligations with capped public support and retailer co-investment, tied to measurable public health outcomes.

D.title: Implementation scope: uniform EU rule vs tailored, risk-based flexibility

D1.title: Uniform EU standard
D1.description: Apply one EU-wide threshold and sampling plan, with minimal derogations, for simplicity and fairness.

D2.title: Harmonized baseline with upward flexibility
D2.description: Define a common minimum baseline for PHC/FSC, allowing Member States or retailers to implement stricter measures if desired.

D3.title: Risk-tailored application
D3.description: Adapt criteria and sampling based on regional risk, flock characteristics, or processor capacity. Allow case-by-case adjustments and SME relief mechanisms.

D4.title: Voluntary adoption & transparency
D4.description: Avoid binding EU-wide rules; instead, rely on voluntary schemes supported by mandatory public reporting to enable consumer-driven accountability.

E.title: Implementation scope: Environmental foodprint of a new foodsafety criteria

E2.title: Intervene with the guideline to reach CO2 equivalent

E3.title: Intervene with the legally binding text to reach CO2 equivalent

relevant_issue_evidence.explanation: The stakeholder repeatedly endorses stricter microbiological criteria, making the type/stringency of the Campylobacter criterion relevant.

relevant_issue_evidence.evidence_quote: Clear labeling and consumer education on safe food handling
relevant_issue_evidence.explanation: The stakeholder emphasizes transparency, labeling, education, and household-level risk reduction, which maps to the supply-chain/control-focus issue.

relevant_issue_evidence.evidence_quote: subsidies to offset potential economic burdens
relevant_issue_evidence.explanation: The stakeholder discusses subsidies, price impacts, household affordability, economic burdens, and food waste, making cost sharing and waste mitigation relevant.

issue_relations.evidence_quote: the health benefits of reducing Campylobacter-related illnesses significantly outweigh these costs
issue_relations.explanation: The stakeholder directly states that public-health benefits from reducing Campylobacter illness outweigh economic costs, supporting greater importance for stricter safety criteria than cost concerns, while still treating costs as relevant.

option_relations.evidence_quote: subsidies to offset potential economic burdens, ensuring equitable access to safer products
option_relations.explanation: The stakeholder supports subsidies to offset burdens and ensure access, which maps to targeted public co-funding. This conflicts with regulated pass-through to consumers, especially given the stakeholder's repeated opposition to price increases limiting access.

uncertainties: The discussion supports stricter microbiological criteria but does not clearly identify which A option is preferred among a lenient phased FSC, a moderate risk-based FSC, or a strict immediate-enforcement FSC.
The stakeholder endorses consumer education, transparency, and labeling, but does not clearly rank B4 against processing-focused, balanced, or environment-focused control strategies.
Beyond support for subsidies and opposition to consumer price increases, the discussion does not clearly rank C1, C4, or C5 relative to C2.
No clear preference evidence is given for implementation scope under issue D or environmental-foodprint intervention under issue E.

The stakeholder emphasizes where controls should be applied along the chain, especially source-based and whole-chain interventions.
The stakeholder treats economic viability and food-waste mitigation as important constraints on implementation.

relevant_issue_evidence.evidence_quote: risk-based interventions throughout the poultry chain
relevant_issue_evidence.explanation: The stakeholder invokes risk-based implementation, which is relevant to the catalogue issue about uniform versus tailored risk-based application.
The stakeholder explicitly raises environmental impacts, EU Green Deal alignment, and sustainability concerns.

issue_relations.evidence_quote: the overarching priority is public health ... outweighing the economic costs associated with stricter controls
issue_relations.explanation: The stakeholder directly states that public-health protection takes priority over economic-cost concerns, mapping public-health-driven stricter criteria to issue A and cost/waste burdens to issue C.

option_relations.explanation: A3 introduces a risk-based FSC aligned with public-health targets, whereas A1 maintains the existing PHC only with no FSC. The stakeholder’s endorsement of stricter criteria supports A3 over the status quo.

option_relations.evidence_quote: ensuring proportionality between public health benefits and economic implications
option_relations.explanation: The stakeholder supports stricter criteria but stresses proportionality, economic viability, and waste mitigation. This maps more clearly to a risk-based moderate FSC with mitigation measures than to immediate strict enforcement focused solely on maximum protection.

option_relations.evidence_quote: throughout the poultry chain, including farm-level biosecurity measures
option_relations.explanation: B3 distributes controls across the chain, including farm-level action. B1 focuses on processing and retail without primarily focusing on on-farm interventions, which is less consistent with the stakeholder’s whole-chain/source-based emphasis.

option_relations.evidence_quote: comprehensive risk management strategies that encompass the entire poultry production chain
option_relations.explanation: The stakeholder prefers comprehensive chain-wide risk management rather than making slaughterhouse and processing controls the main focus, supporting B3 over B2.

option_relations.evidence_quote: dynamic shelf-life management to reduce unnecessary food waste
option_relations.explanation: The stakeholder specifically endorses waste-reduction tools such as dynamic shelf-life management and rejects disproportionate burdens. This maps better to C4’s waste-minimization toolkit than to C1’s full producer liability and standard disposal approach.

uncertainties: The discussion supports stricter criteria, but it does not clearly distinguish between a phased lenient FSC and a moderate risk-based FSC beyond the general preference for balanced, evidence-based stringency.
The stakeholder emphasizes source-based and whole-chain controls, but the catalogue does not contain a purely farm/source-first option; B3 is only an approximate mapping.
The stakeholder discusses economic viability and industry adaptation but does not specify subsidies, retailer co-investment, cost pass-through, or a precise cost-sharing model among C2, C3, and C5.

The stakeholder uses risk-based language, but does not clearly state whether implementation should be a uniform EU rule, a harmonized baseline with flexibility, or tailored regional/processor-specific application.
Environmental concerns are relevant, but the stakeholder does not specify whether CO2-equivalent goals should be pursued through non-binding guidelines or legally binding text.
